notes: Strategic-grill is a conversational, multi-turn skill. These evals test the FIRST response only. Iteration 2 changes: (1) evals 2 and 3 now pre-seed a minimal context-file structure so the technique must appear in the Q:/Recommendation block instead of being deferred behind the cold-start housekeeping question; (2) eval 10's ownership assertion is broadened; (3) eval 14's assertions are reframed to reward the skill's correct behaviour (keep DDD labels out of conversation, defer the YAML write) instead of demanding a literal label in turn 1; (4) added discriminating assertions — no-DDD-jargon-in-user-text, canonical-labels-only, and no-implementation-leakage — on the evals where plain-Opus baselines leaked these.

evals.name: cold-start-plain-language
evals.prompt: I'm building a SaaS tool for restaurant inventory management. We need to track ingredients, suppliers, and orders. Help me think through how to structure this.
evals.expected_output: Skill notices there are no existing context files, asks (or proposes) a documentation file structure, and asks a single sharp grilling question in plain business language about what makes the product unique.
expectations: Asks exactly one grilling question; a single procedural file-layout question is allowed because no docs exist yet, but no other grilling questions are bundled in
The grilling question uses the Q:/Recommendation format with a concrete recommendation (not 'it depends')
Uses plain business language with NO DDD jargon (bounded context, ubiquitous language, subdomain, anti-corruption layer, ACL, core domain) anywhere in the user-facing text
Because no CONTEXT files exist, it proposes or asks about a documentation file structure before capturing decisions
Keeps implementation details (DB schemas, table layouts, tech-stack choices) out of the response — stays at the level of what the product is and what makes it unique

evals.name: fuzzy-language-member
evals.prompt: We have accounts, users, and customers in our system, and now I want to add a 'member' concept for people who've paid for a subscription. Walk me through it.
evals.expected_output: Skill reads the existing glossary (which already defines account/user/customer), then uses its first Q:/Recommendation block to sharpen the fuzzy 'member' term against those existing terms.
expectations: Shows evidence of reading the existing glossary that defines account, user, and customer
The Q:/Recommendation block itself works to disambiguate 'member' against the existing terms (the sharpening is the question, not an aside)
Asks exactly one focused question — no bundled questions
Uses the Q:/Recommendation format with a concrete recommendation
Uses plain business language with NO DDD jargon in the user-facing text
Does not re-ask about file structure, since context docs already exist

evals.name: weak-core-claim-pushback
evals.prompt: Our notification service is the core of our platform — it's what users love about us. I want to make sure we structure the rest of the system around it.
evals.expected_output: Skill reads the existing contexts, then uses its first Q:/Recommendation block to push back directly on the 'notifications is core' claim rather than deferring it.
expectations: Shows evidence of reading the existing contexts (Orders / Customers)
Challenges the 'notifications is core' claim directly in the Q:/Recommendation block — not merely teed up in surrounding prose for a later turn
References off-the-shelf alternatives or competitive differentiation (e.g. what would be lost if replaced with SendGrid / Twilio)
The recommendation leans toward classifying notifications as supporting/generic unless a specific non-replicable capability is named
Uses the Q:/Recommendation format, in plain business language with NO DDD jargon in the user-facing text

evals.name: new-feature-loyalty-points
evals.prompt: I want to add a loyalty points system to our platform — customers earn points on orders and redeem them. How should we fit this in?
evals.expected_output: Skill reads the existing context files, asks whether loyalty is a new area or part of an existing one, in plain language, without leaking jargon, invented labels, or implementation detail.
expectations: Shows evidence of reading the existing context files (references Orders and/or Customers by name or documented definition)
Asks whether loyalty points should be a new context/area or live inside an existing one (Customers or Orders)
Uses the Q:/Recommendation format with a concrete recommendation
Does not re-ask about file structure, since context files already exist
Uses plain business language with NO DDD jargon in the user-facing text
If it proposes a relationship label, it uses only canonical DDD patterns (Customer-Supplier, ACL, Open Host Service, etc.) and does NOT invent labels such as 'Publisher-Subscriber'
Keeps implementation details (DB schemas, points-ledger/table design) out — artifacts stay glossaries, not specs

evals.name: cross-context-reporting-dashboard
evals.prompt: We want to build a reporting dashboard that pulls data from Orders, Inventory, and Customers to show business KPIs. Where should it live?
evals.expected_output: Skill reads the existing contexts and raises the ownership/boundary concern for a feature that reads across three contexts, in plain language, staying at the boundary level.
expectations: Shows evidence of reading the existing context files (references Orders, Inventory, and/or Customers)
Raises the question of ownership or boundaries for a feature that reads across multiple existing contexts
Uses the Q:/Recommendation format with a concrete recommendation
Treats reporting as likely a separate context rather than silently embedding it in one of the three
Uses plain business language with NO DDD jargon in the user-facing text
Keeps implementation details (ETL/event-store/query mechanics) out — stays at the ownership/boundary level

evals.name: relationship-change-shipping-inventory
evals.prompt: We want the Shipping service to update Inventory stock levels directly whenever items ship out. Sounds simple enough, right?
evals.expected_output: Skill reads the existing Shipping/Inventory relationship and flags that the proposed direct write inverts the documented ownership, in plain language.
expectations: Shows evidence of reading the existing relationship between Shipping and Inventory from the context map
Flags that letting Shipping write to Inventory directly conflicts with or changes the documented relationship (Inventory is upstream / owns its model)
Uses the Q:/Recommendation format with a concrete recommendation
Does not simply agree that it 'sounds simple' — surfaces the ownership/coupling consequence
Uses plain business language with NO DDD jargon (e.g. spells out 'translation layer' rather than dropping 'ACL') in the user-facing text

evals.name: boundary-expansion-subscriptions
evals.prompt: We want to move subscription management into our User module — users are the ones with subscriptions anyway, so it makes sense to keep them together.
evals.expected_output: Skill reads the narrowly-scoped User context and challenges the boundary expansion, in plain language.
expectations: Shows evidence of reading the existing User context and its documented (narrow) scope
Challenges folding subscriptions into the User module rather than accepting the 'makes sense to keep them together' reasoning
The challenge references a real distinction (different lifecycle, different owner, billing concern vs identity concern)
Uses the Q:/Recommendation format with a concrete recommendation
Uses plain business language with NO DDD jargon in the user-facing text

evals.name: new-cross-cutting-refund-flow
evals.prompt: I want to add a refund flow. It touches payments, orders, and inventory since we have to reverse the charge, mark the order, and restock items.
evals.expected_output: Skill reads the three existing contexts and surfaces who owns/orchestrates the refund before diving into mechanics, in plain language, staying at the boundary level.
expectations: Shows evidence of reading the existing Payments, Orders, and/or Inventory contexts
Surfaces who owns/orchestrates the refund (a single owning context driving the others) before mechanics — whether by asking new-context-vs-existing or which existing context owns it
Uses the Q:/Recommendation format with a concrete recommendation
Stays at the boundary/ownership level and does not jump into implementation mechanics (saga/compensation, warehouse resolution, per-field schema)
Uses plain business language with NO DDD jargon in the user-facing text

evals.name: stale-path-detection
evals.prompt: Here's our setup. I want to add fraud detection to the payments area. Where should it go?
evals.expected_output: Skill cross-checks the path: entries in CONTEXT-MAP.yaml against the real codebase, notices the billing path is stale (the directory is actually 'payments'), and flags the mismatch before grilling.
expectations: Cross-checks the paths listed in CONTEXT-MAP.yaml against the actual directories present in the codebase
Flags that a referenced path is stale or missing (the map points to a billing directory that doesn't exist; the real one is payments)
Surfaces this mismatch to the user rather than silently proceeding
Still moves toward the user's actual question (where fraud detection should go) after flagging the mismatch

evals.name: glossary-term-conflict
evals.prompt: I want to add orders to our supplier management — basically we need to send orders to suppliers to restock inventory.
evals.expected_output: Skill notices that 'order' already has a customer-facing definition in the glossary and challenges the term conflict, proposing a distinct term (e.g. Purchase Order).
expectations: Shows evidence of reading the existing glossary where 'Order' is defined as a customer-facing concept
Flags the conflict between the user's supplier-facing 'order' and the existing customer-facing 'Order' term
Proposes a distinct term for the supplier-facing concept (e.g. Purchase Order, Restock Order, Supplier Order)
Uses the Q:/Recommendation format with a concrete recommendation

evals.name: relationship-labelling
evals.prompt: Our Notifications area reads order events from the Orders area and sends emails when an order ships. How should I record that the two are connected?
evals.expected_output: Skill identifies this as a single one-directional relationship to record, recommends one integration shape, and conveys the team-autonomy implication — in plain language, keeping raw DDD labels out of the conversation and not proposing several patterns at once.
expectations: Shows evidence of reading the existing Orders and Notifications contexts
Identifies it as a single one-directional relationship to record (Orders as the source/upstream, Notifications as the consumer/downstream) rather than vaguely 'connected'
Conveys the team-autonomy implication of the recommended shape (e.g. a translation layer lets the core Orders context change without breaking Notifications)
Keeps user-facing language plain — does not dump raw DDD label names, invent non-canonical labels, or propose several patterns at once
Uses the Q:/Recommendation format with a concrete recommendation about which integration shape to use
